demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
Marcus's Mornings

Marcus sits in the consultation room with his hands folded in his lap, a habit he's developed over the past eighteen months. He's a slender man with dark eyes that rarely make contact, dressed in the kind of carefully coordinated outfit that speaks to his profession—a charcoal linen shirt, tailored trousers, shoes that match his belt. His wife Priya sometimes jokes that he color-coordinates his anxiety. Today, he's chosen grays and blacks.

Nineteen months ago, Marcus's father died suddenly of a massive heart attack while Marcus was at work. They were supposed to have lunch that Saturday. His father had called that morning with a new recipe idea for their family's traditional dal, something he wanted to discuss with Marcus over food. Marcus had said yes, but then a client emergency came up—a high-end residential project with difficult contractors. He rescheduled for the following week. His father collapsed in the kitchen two hours before they would have met.

When the police called, Marcus was on a video conference, discussing paint finishes and fabric swatches. He remembers the fluorescent office lights, the way his colleague's face froze on the monitor when he stood up. He remembers thinking, with a strange clarity that still disturbs him, that his father's death was inconvenient.

Now Marcus wakes at 4:47 every morning, always before his alarm. His heart rate climbs as consciousness returns. He lies in the darkness next to Priya, who sleeps deeply, mercifully unaware of the way his chest tightens as he waits for something terrible to happen. By 5:30, he's usually in the kitchen, moving quietly, checking that the stove is off multiple times even though he hasn't used it. He's learned not to turn on the lights—the darkness feels safer somehow, less likely to trigger the cascade of images that have become unwelcome companions.

His work has suffered in ways that are hard to articulate to clients. He designs beautiful spaces—it's what he's always done, what he's known since childhood when he would rearrange his parents' living room furniture, earning his father's delighted laughter. But now, when he's selecting colors for a master bedroom or envisioning a family dining area, his mind fractures. He'll be holding a fabric sample and suddenly he's thinking about his father's kitchen, the one where he collapsed, and Marcus can't breathe properly. He's missed deadlines. He's had to excuse himself from meetings. One client complained about his "distracted demeanor."

Priya has been patient, but he can feel the weight of it. She's stopped inviting him to her work functions. She eats dinner alone most nights while he sits in their perfectly designed living room—a space he now finds suffocating—scrolling through his phone, unable to focus on anything. He's looked at his father's contact information perhaps two hundred times, his thumb hovering over the name before remembering, again, that the line is dead.

What troubles Marcus most is the guilt that lives beneath everything else. He didn't go to lunch. He chose work. And now, when his mother calls, he feels a spike of panic—an irrational certainty that she's calling with more bad news. He's begun avoiding her calls. This makes him feel like a terrible son, which makes the guilt heavier, which makes sleep even more impossible.

He tells his therapist that he doesn't know how to live in a world where he was supposed to have lunch with his father and didn't, and now never will.
